title: 1997 AHSME Problem 29
statement: Call a positive real number special if it has a decimal representation that consists entirely of digits \(0\) and \(7.\) For example, \(\frac{700}{99}=7.07=7.070707\ldots\) and \(77.007\) are special numbers. What is the smallest \(n\) such that \(1\) can be written as a sum of \(n\) special numbers?

answerChoices.label: E
answerChoices.text:
\(1\) cannot be represented as a sum of finitely many special
numbers

solutions.text: Suppose \(1\) is a sum of \(n\) special numbers, and let \(a_k\) count summands having a \(7\) in the \(k\)th decimal place. Dividing by \(7\) gives \[ \begin{aligned} \frac17&=\frac{a_1}{10}+\frac{a_2}{10^2}+\cdots\\ &=0.\overline{142857}. \end{aligned} \] For \(n\le9,\) each \(a_k\) is a digit, so \(a_1,a_2,\ldots=1,4,2,8,5,7,\ldots;\) hence \(n\ge8.\) Eight suffice because the repeating special decimals represented by \[ \begin{aligned} 700700+2(070707)\\ {}+2(077777)\\ {}+3(000777)&=999999. \end{aligned} \] Their sum is \(1.\) Therefore the minimum is \(8,\) and B is correct.
hints: If \(a_k\) summands have \(7\) in decimal place \(k\), divide the sum by \(7\)
Compare the resulting digit counts with the repeating decimal for \(\frac{1}{7}\), then seek a six-digit repeating construction
